# QM Basic: Course overview {#basic-course}

QM Basic is about deciding with data when you do not have all the facts.
Can you trust a survey of 40 friends? How many sandwiches should your lunch
startup make for tomorrow? Is your average order value really above break-even, or was the high average
just luck?
Each lecture starts from a question like these and tries to answer it with
data. Then it gives you the theory you need to understand the answer and to
check it. This works in the same way when the answer comes from R and when it
comes from an AI assistant. We begin by describing data. Then we build simple
models of chance. We end with confidence intervals and tests.

::: {.outcomes}
<span class="label">By the end of QM Basic, you can</span>

- identify observational units, variables, samples, populations, and the
  limits that come from how the data were selected
- summarise and visualise quantitative and categorical data in R
- work with events, random variables, distributions, expectation, variance,
  covariance, and correlation
- update a probability when new information arrives (conditioning and Bayes' rule)
- use uniform, normal, and t models and check the conditions under which
  each model applies
- explain sampling variability, standard errors, confidence intervals, and
  two-sided tests of a claimed value
- interpret supplied R output with correct units, uncertainty, scope, and
  causal limits.
:::

## Course sequence

| Chapter | Main focus |
|---|---|
| Lecture 1 | Introduction to data analysis |
| Lecture 2 | Probability foundations and random variables |
| Lecture 3 | Discrete distributions, expectation, and variance |
| Tutorial 1 | Evidence and probability foundations |
| Lecture 4 | Conditioning, Bayes' rule, and independence |
| Lecture 5 | Joint random variables, covariance, and correlation |
| Tutorial 2 | Conditioning and relationships |
| Lecture 6 | Continuous distributions and the normal model |
| Lecture 7 | Samples, parameters, and estimators |
| Lecture 8 | Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem |
| Lecture 9 | The t distribution and confidence intervals |
| Tutorial 3 | Normal models, sampling, and confidence intervals |
| Lecture 10 | Testing decisions, errors, power, and a first look at regression |
| Tutorial 4 | Hypothesis tests, errors, and power |
| Formula sheet | Formulas of Lectures 1--10, attached to the exam |
| Mock exam | 100-point practice exam on the whole course |

## How to read every graph

Use the same sequence whenever a graph appears:

1. **Unit and variables.** What does one observation represent, and what is
   on each axis, in which units?
2. **Scales.** Read the axis scales: where they start, how wide each interval
   is, and whether the vertical axis shows a count or a proportion.
3. **One element.** Describe one bar, point, or line in a full sentence.
4. **Pattern.** Describe the overall shape before you interpret it.
5. **Limits.** State one thing the graph cannot tell you.

## The weekly rhythm

Both QM courses follow the same weekly routine, with a time budget for each
step: prepare before class, take part in class, read and practise after class. The [How to succeed in this course](../resources/how-to-succeed.qmd)
page lays out the week, day by day, with printable checklists.

## Tutorials and assessment

Four tutorials help you prepare for the exam with guided practice. Bring your
attempts at the after-class questions, and use the cumulative
[QM Basic Formula Sheet](formula-sheet.qmd) during each tutorial. The
complete sheet is attached to the closed-book written exam. The few
multipliers you need, such as 1.96 in a 95% confidence interval, are on the
formula sheet or in the question. You do not need the large printed tables of
statistical distributions.

The [QM Basic Mock Exam](mock-exam.qmd) has the same form as the real exam:
seven open questions with 100 points in 180 minutes. You calculate, you
interpret supplied R output, and you assess an answer from an AI assistant.
